parsed.rationale: The speech argues against a bill regulating Roman Catholic convents and alleged forcible detention of women (nuns), focusing on religious liberty, hearsay evidence, and visitation of convents. It does not address women’s political rights or representation (suffrage, eligibility for office, civic duties like jury service, or access to professions) nor women’s fitness for political participation.

The speech advocates increasing women’s participation in science and engineering education and careers and the collection of gender-disaggregated data by the Learning and Skills Council. It does not address women’s political rights or representation (voting, holding office, political structures), nor women’s distinctive civic duties. Therefore it is outside the defined scope.

The speech debates income tax enforcement and marital property liabilities—whether a husband’s goods can be distrained for a wife’s tax debts. It only mentions “votes for women” in passing without taking a position. There is no substantive argument for or against women’s political rights or representation.

The speaker opposes removing the disqualification of married women voters, derides the proposal as a “tremendous change” and a bill to “turn women into men,” and disparages women’s participation in public life. While he makes a rhetorical concession that there might be arguments for giving political privileges to married women, he does not endorse it; instead he objects to granting rights, particularly to separated married women, and argues such changes should not be made. Overall, he argues against expanding women’s political rights in this context.

The speech concerns unemployment relief and welfare measures (boots, clothing, school feeding, nourishment) for women and children in distressed mining areas, without arguing about women’s voting rights, eligibility for office, representation structures, or civic duties.

The speaker argues that pledges for women’s suffrage are worthless, that once the issue became real Members avoided voting on it, that major reforms require a unified party to take responsibility (which suffrage lacks), and that there is no majority among male voters and no one would fight an election on female suffrage. These points present women’s suffrage as lacking mandate and viability, indicating opposition.

The speaker explicitly supports enfranchising women, calling their exclusion a “scandal and disgrace” and hoping women’s suffrage will be included when reforming the franchise. This is a clear endorsement of women’s political rights.

The target speech focuses on South-East Asian foreign policy, SEATO, recognition of China, the Geneva Accords, and the International Supervisory Commission in Vietnam. It does not argue for or against women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation mechanisms, or women’s distinct civic duties. Any mentions of men/women are incidental and not about political rights.

The speaker argues in favor of the Women’s Suffrage Bill, rejects the mandate objection, asserts the House should lead public opinion, questions claims of public indignation against suffrage, and notes MPs have supported women’s suffrage without electoral penalty.

The speaker argues that women are qualified to chair School Boards and should be eligible to be elected chair of District Councils, supports giving councils the unrestricted choice to elect a woman, rejects claims women wouldn’t be interested, and states this would aid woman suffrage by proving women’s fitness to vote. This is clear support for women’s political rights and representation.

The speaker strongly advocates women’s suffrage, arguing it is anomalous to exclude women by sex, invokes “no taxation without representation,” rebuts objections (military service, capacity, political interest), cites examples of capable women, and urges immediate enfranchisement. No substantive opposition is presented.

The speaker questions process and mandate, advocating a referendum and objecting to using this amendment under the Parliament Act, but explicitly states he would support a large measure of women’s suffrage if adopted and that his present opposition is due to procedural/constitutional concerns rather than principle. He votes against now but emphasizes retaining freedom to support in future—procedural objection, not substantive opposition to women’s political rights.

The speech focuses on education policy (assisted places, comprehensive schools, school meals, and transport). A brief mention that more women worked during WWII is incidental and not about women’s political rights, representation, or civic status. No argument for or against women’s political rights is made.

The target text discusses a Scottish housing bill (overcrowding standards, rents, reconditioning, local authority powers). Women are mentioned only incidentally (a woman member of Glasgow Corporation; “working-man’s wife”; and the speaker saying she is not an advocate of women’s rights). There is no argument for or against women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, or structures of political representation.

The target speech focuses on parliamentary procedure and scrutiny of Supplementary Estimates, using various spending examples (including a brief mention of benefits for disabled married women) to argue for debate time. It does not make an argument about women’s voting rights, eligibility for office, representation structures, or women’s civic status; the gendered benefit example is welfare-related and out of scope.

The speech addresses postwar economic policy, industrial relations, trade unions, and cost of living. Women are mentioned only incidentally (as workers during wartime dilution and as housewives) with no argument about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation mechanisms, or distinctive civic duties. Hence it is not about women’s political rights or representation.

The speaker only asks clarifying questions about whether the clause would increase the number of women electors and how it affects soldiers’ wives, without advocating for or against women’s political rights. No substantive position is taken.

The speaker urges acceptance of an amendment to ensure women in India receive the recommended voting power/proportion after the first election, or at least an assurance that promises to women will be fulfilled—clearly advocating for women’s suffrage/representation.

The speaker positively references improving representation of women and ethnic minorities in Parliament and suggests term limits to increase turnover and make Parliament more representative. This endorses greater women’s political representation, aligning with support for women’s political rights/representation.

No substantive opposing arguments are offered in the TARGET text.
The target speech only notes that another member seemed to support extending jury service to all women; the speaker does not express any stance on women’s political rights or jury service themselves.

The speech concerns education policy and the role of clergy in schools. It contains only an incidental mention of "serving women" and makes no argument about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation, or other civic rights.

The quota proposal is a clear endorsement of women’s participation in public bodies, i.e., political representation within the scope. No opposing arguments are made.

The speech concerns funding and structure of Irish national education, mixed vs denominational schooling, model schools, and teacher salaries. It does not argue for or against women’s suffrage, political representation, eligibility for office, or civic duties. A brief mention of female teachers’ salaries is not framed as an argument about women’s political rights or equal civic status.

Supports increasing women’s representation, backs the bill to enable positive action, and urges his party to use it (e.g., aiming for ~50% women on candidate lists). He opposes women-only shortlists but that is a procedural/mechanism objection, not opposition to women’s political rights.

Although he would have preferred women’s suffrage for Ireland to be decided by an Irish Parliament, that is a procedural/nationalist caveat rather than substantive opposition. Overall stance is supportive of women’s political rights.

The speaker explicitly states opposition to Women’s Suffrage (“as I am opposed to it”) and condemns suffrage meetings as a scandal and disgrace, arguing against the movement and implying they should be curtailed.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as a strong anti-suffragist for the Imperial Parliament, opposing women's suffrage there, but states he would not object to Women Suffrage for a local Scottish Parliament and even suggests that is the only part of the Bill he might favor. He also mocks the notion of married women’s household qualification, reinforcing skepticism. This constitutes substantive positions both for (at local level) and against (at Imperial level) women’s political rights.

The speaker strongly supports women’s political representation, endorsing mainstreaming equality, arguing that democracy requires representative chambers, praising positive action that led to more Labour women MPs, and advocating gender-balanced candidate lists for the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly.

The speaker argues about procedural order and the definition/scope of “political funds,” mentioning the Suffragist League only as an example among other organizations. There is no argument for or against women’s political rights or representation.

The speech addresses foreign policy expenditures, Turkish prisoners in Malta, and relief for Russian/Anglo-Russian refugees. References to women are incidental (e.g., a committee for training women) and do not concern voting, holding office, representation, or women’s civic status. No argument is made about women’s political rights.

The speech focuses on juvenile delinquency, media influence, and proposing youth voluntary service opportunities. It does not discuss women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation mechanisms, or women’s distinct civic rights or duties; mentions of “men and women” are incidental and not about political rights.

The speaker praises policies as empowering working women and explicitly calls for more women to enter Parliament, aiming for 51% representation, which is a clear endorsement of women’s political representation.

The speech focuses on social security and incapacity benefit reforms, noting impacts on women working part-time, and references to child benefit history. It does not argue for or against women’s political rights, representation, or civic status; mentions of women are incidental to welfare policy.

The speech debates church vs. popular control in school management and denominational education; it does not argue about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, or women’s distinct civic status. Mentions of “men and women” are incidental to competence for school management, not political rights.

The speaker argues that government bodies and committees dealing with women’s issues are dominated by men and calls for women’s inclusion in executive and policy-making roles, decries prejudice against employing women, urges stronger action to ensure women’s access to work (including penalties on employers who refuse women), and advocates for women’s participation in defense roles (Home Guard). These are clear endorsements of expanding women’s role and representation in public decision-making and civic duties.

The target text is a multi-speaker debate focused on the Manchester (Peterloo) meeting, the Riot Act, legality of assemblies, calls for parliamentary inquiry, and general parliamentary reform. References to women are incidental (as victims in the crowd or a hypothetical “old women” example), not about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, or gender-specific civic status. Therefore, it does not argue for or against women’s political rights.

The speaker criticizes Mr. Stansfeld for pushing women’s suffrage, calling it an attempt to enforce the “despotism of Democracy” and framing it negatively as forcing the Prime Minister to adopt a policy he opposes. This language signals clear opposition to women’s suffrage.

The speech discusses Northern Ireland border security, examining officers, identity documentation, and identity cards. It makes no argument about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation, or any policy singling out women’s civic status.

The target speech concerns the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts and proposes maintaining/expanding hospital accommodation and treatment for women (including possible detention until cured). It is a public health and morality discussion about prostitution and disease control in garrison towns, not about women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, representation, or distinctive civic duties. Therefore it does not argue for or against women’s political rights or representation.

The speech critiques the Finance Bill and Selective Employment Tax, with a section on reducing tax burdens for married women to encourage employment. While it addresses women’s taxation and labor participation, it does not argue about women’s political rights or representation (franchise, eligibility for office, quotas, jury service, etc.). Hence it is out of scope for women’s political rights stance classification.

The speaker supports women’s participation under equal conditions and rights when called to the Forces and provides options across Auxiliary Services, Civil Defence, and industry, but also argues to exempt married women from compulsory military service (while allowing direction to employment) and to avoid directing mothers away from home. This is substantive support for inclusion alongside substantive exemptions, i.e., mixed stance.

The target speech focuses on criticizing the Government’s franchise bill and Liberal Party dynamics. Women’s suffrage is only mentioned briefly as a rhetorical jab—Churchill challenges Hartington to repudiate the bill because it omits female suffrage, attributing that view to Hartington; Hartington then denies having mentioned women’s suffrage. Neither speaker advances a substantive argument for or against women’s political rights.

The speech concerns social security/pension rules (abolishing the married women’s half test and discussing a quarter test and publicity). Although it jokingly mentions the “women’s vote,” it makes no argument about women’s political rights, suffrage, eligibility for office, or structures of representation. Hence it is not about women’s political rights.

The speaker explicitly condemns discrimination against women in immigration law (1971 Act) and criticizes the Bill for lowering men’s rights rather than giving women equal rights, thereby advocating equal rights for women in this policy area. Other content is about immigration/race, but on women’s rights the stance is pro-equality.

The target speech focuses on election-day transport (motor cars) and polling facilities, with a humorous aside about young married women. It does not argue for or against women’s suffrage, eligibility for office, or distinct civic duties; it merely assumes women vote. Therefore, it is not an argument about women’s political rights or representation.

The target speech explicitly endorses the principle of “one man or one woman, one vote” and supports the Bill for abolishing plural voting—clear support for equal franchise including women. While a subsequent speaker criticizes the Bill on electoral grounds and discusses business and university votes, he does not argue against women’s political rights; his mentions of women are incidental. Overall, the target contains a substantive pro-women’s-rights argument without substantive opposition.

The speaker defends forcible feeding of hunger-striking prisoners and recounts a paradox about suffragette slogans but does not argue for or against women’s suffrage or their political rights; the vote is only mentioned anecdotally.

The speaker declares himself a convinced suffragist, says extension of the franchise to women would be good, and intends to vote for it on the forthcoming Franchise Bill. However, he opposes applying women’s suffrage via this Home Rule Bill amendment to Ireland now, arguing there is no effective demand among Irish women and that it could imperil Home Rule and would be imposed without their desire. He supports suffrage in general but opposes it for Irish women in this specific context/timing, thus taking substantive positions on both sides.

The speaker’s brief reference to “female franchise” is used only as a rhetorical example to question the Government’s vague criterion of “capable citizens,” not to advocate for or against women’s suffrage. He neither endorses nor opposes women’s political rights; the main argument concerns franchise expansion and redistribution timing/mechanism.

The speaker vehemently opposes the Contagious Diseases Acts as unjust, gender-discriminatory laws targeting women, calls for their repeal, argues that any law should be equal between sexes, condemns male-only Parliament imposing degrading treatment on women, and highlights the injustice toward poor women. This supports women’s civil rights and equal legal treatment.

The speech focuses on factory inspection, workplace safety, and the need for more female inspectors. It mentions “the sort of argument used by the Prime Minister against female suffrage” only as an analogy to criticize reliance on male inspectors, without making a substantive argument for or against women’s voting rights or political representation. Thus it does not take a stance on women’s political rights.

The TARGET includes a strong speech opposing the Amendment and explicitly arguing that women should “leave government now to men,” asserting inherent “limitations” of women and warning against upsetting the social balance—clear opposition to women’s political participation. Although a subsequent speaker supports equal compensation for women, that concerns wartime injury compensation (largely out of scope for political rights). The in-scope content is the explicit anti-participation stance, so overall the TARGET is against women’s political rights.

The speech debates labour regulations (two-shift system, night work for women and young persons) and administrative authority between departments, not women’s political rights, suffrage, eligibility for office, or civic duties. Mentions of women concern employment conditions rather than political representation or civic status.

The speaker criticizes the Government for introducing a franchise (Plural Voting) bill while not allowing or offering an alternative to include a Women’s Suffrage amendment, noting public dissatisfaction. This implies support for providing a path to women’s suffrage and treats the Government’s failure to do so as regrettable.

The target advocates ensuring adequate representation of women on the college council, and the minister’s reply indicates no barrier to appointing more women—both aligning with support for women’s representation.

The speech focuses on limiting the Home Secretary’s discretion to release prisoners on health grounds and on deterring hunger-striking prisoners (including suffragists). References to women’s suffrage ("give votes to all sorts of women") are hypothetical and incidental, not substantive arguments for or against women’s political rights. Thus, it does not take a clear stance on women’s political rights or representation.

The speech centers on Church Commissioners’ finances, secrecy, pensions, and legislative procedure (Bill vs Measure). Its only gender-related content is support for women’s ordination and criticism of linked compensation—an internal Church matter about religious office, not women’s civic or political rights (vote, stand for public office, representation). Therefore it does not argue about women’s political rights.

The speaker opposes the Equal Franchise Bill that would enfranchise women at 21 because it would create a female majority and “permanent political supremacy,” calling it bad statesmanship and inequality. However, he proposes a “constitutional solution” to give votes to women only down to an age that would keep male and female electorates approximately equal, to which he raises no objection. Thus he supports limited/partial enfranchisement for women while opposing full equal political rights that produce a female numerical majority.

The speaker comments procedurally on referring the idea of women’s suffrage in India back to Indian opinion and suggests adjourning to gauge demand, without expressing substantive support or opposition to women’s political rights. The remark about “one vote for every woman” is a mischaracterization, not a clear stance. Overall, no direct argument for or against women’s political rights is made.

The speaker argues that the bill chiefly affects women and that “we, as men, have no right to pass” it, warning against interfering with women’s liberties without knowing whether Parliament correctly represents women’s views. This implicitly supports women’s political representation/voice in policymaking. No substantive opposition to women’s rights is expressed.

The speaker backs strengthening the Sex Discrimination Bill and empowering the Equal Opportunities Commission to issue guidelines to prevent discrimination, explicitly positioning this as helping women (e.g., “ordinary working women”) and criticizing the Government for not accepting amendments. Any reservations are procedural, not opposition to women’s rights.

The speech advocates for direct election of the Prime Minister and constitutional reform. It mentions opposition to votes for women only as a historical analogy, without making any substantive argument about women’s political rights or representation.

The speaker positively references women’s suffrage and proposes honoring suffragettes, and substantively supports maintaining independent taxation for married women—a policy explicitly concerning women’s distinct status under tax law—without presenting opposing arguments. Other topics raised are socio-economic and largely out of scope for political rights, but the tax point is in-scope and supportive.

The speaker rejects an amendment to expand Burmese women’s franchise via husbands’ qualifications, citing administrative/organizational difficulties and arguing that a 1:3.5 women-to-men elector ratio is acceptable and not an injustice. This is opposition to further women’s political rights in this context, not balanced by substantive pro-expansion arguments.

The speaker supports women serving as councillors and aldermen (including via co-optation) and will vote against an amendment that would exclude them, but explicitly opposes women serving as mayors (since mayors are magistrates ex officio). This is support for some offices and opposition to another.

The speaker argues against paragraph (c) by highlighting that, while current double registrations don’t yield two votes at general elections, the Bill would newly enfranchise 30,000 women via spousal/business grounds and grant a second vote to about 100,000 women—i.e., it would create many plural voters. This is a substantive objection to expanding women’s voting rights in this specific form (plural/spousal franchise).

Within the TARGET, Mr. J. R. Kelly derides a “women’s suffrage Amendment” and disparages women ratepayers as “few widows and scatter-brained spinsters,” dismissing their authority to represent other women. This is a clear negative stance toward women’s political representation; no substantive pro-suffrage argument is offered in the TARGET.

The speaker invokes women’s newly granted franchise, insisting it would be an "absolute outrage" to pass the divorce reform before women have had the chance to pronounce on it at the ballot box, thereby affirming women’s political voice. He also references supporting equality between the sexes. This constitutes support for women’s political rights/representation.

The speaker supports granting Parliamentary votes to women, but only to those already on the municipal (local government) register, and opposes the amendment that would extend the vote on the same residential basis as men. Thus, they endorse a restricted subset while opposing a broader extension.

The speaker states he voted for women councillors last year and would repeat that vote, indicating support for women’s eligibility for local office. His opposition here is procedural/practical—arguing the House should not overturn last year’s settlement within 12 months and that the Bill cannot progress late in the session—rather than substantive opposition to women’s political participation. Although he says the case for women inspectors is stronger than for councillors, he does not reject women councillors on merit.

The speaker argues for bona fide qualifications to prevent ‘faggot voting’ and explicitly includes women as legitimate voters if they meet the ratepayer/residence standard (“man or woman… should also be a ratepayer”). He does not oppose women’s suffrage; his concerns are procedural/anti-gerrymandering, supporting women’s participation under proper qualifications.

The speaker explicitly advocates expanding women’s roles in the Armed Forces, proposing that many support and administrative functions be done by women (e.g., Engineers’ survey, movement control, postal, supplies, barrack services, ordnance, and especially the Pay Corps). This supports increased participation and access to public service roles for women, with no substantive opposition presented.
